---
title: "'Rethinking STI Policy: Innovation Ecosystems, Metrics and Society', a MultiObs seminar"
date: 2026-11-20
categories: [Seminar]
---

The MultiObs program (Multi-Observatory of Science, Technology and Innovation Dynamics), of the São Paulo Excellence Chair, held on November 18th a hybrid seminar titled ['Rethinking STI Policy: Innovation Ecosystems, Metrics and Society'](https://www.multiobs.org/events/multiobs-seminar-rethinking-sti-policy-innovation-ecosystems-metrics-and-society). Victoria Di Césare, our team member, joined the online call to listen to presentations by renowned researchers in the field.

The programme included an "Overview of the MultiObs Project" by Rodrigo Costas, the talk "Beyond the Silicon Valley Archetype: Measuring the Dynamics of Place-Based Innovation" by Nicholas Vonortas, and a discussion about "Alignment and misalignment between research agendas and societal needs. Why diversity and inclusion matter" by Ismael Rafols. On behalf of the MultiObs initiative, Dr. Costas argued for a better Scientometrics that develops more inclusive, diverse, and contextualised indicators. He also highlighted the importance of codevelopment and participatory approaches that include those traditionally left out of the conversation regarding scientific infrastructure and assessment.

Next, Prof. Vonortas presented Silicon Valley as an irreplicable case, even within the US context, and explained different ways to measure and evaluate territorial innovation ecosystems. Currently, there are several studies funded by the NSF to assess knowledge-intensive entrepreneurs across the country. Finally, Dr. Ràfols closed the seminar with a talk about the misalignment between science supply and societal demands. He made the case for maintaining a balance between prioritisation and epistemic diversity in research funding, without losing sight of the specific social contexts involved. A key takeaway from this seminar for Victoria was that scientific research creates capabilities, not direct solutions to societal problems. And that is where policy must step in.
